title: 人工智能，从零搭建 · 第19部分：推断

chapters.Outro: 回顾，以及这些想法从何而来

d5f3852185fd.en: When a big model writes, it writes one token at a time. And to write each one, it has to read every single one of its weights. <bookmark mark='a'/> For a seventy-billion-parameter model, stored as sixteen-bit numbers, two bytes each, that's a hundred and forty-one gigabytes, streamed from memory through to the chip, <bookmark mark='b'/> for one token. Then all of it again for the next one, and the next. <bookmark mark='c'/> How many bytes a second can flow from memory to the chip is the memory bandwidth: here, three point three five terabytes a second.

489a66bfcca3.en: So memory sets a speed limit. Tokens per second can't beat the memory bandwidth divided by the bytes of weights: on one of today's best chips, about 24 tokens a second. <bookmark mark='a'/> And meanwhile the chip's arithmetic sits almost idle. <bookmark mark='b'/> One conversation uses a third of one percent of it. <bookmark mark='c'/> Running a trained model to get answers, with no learning, just using it, is called inference; it's not part six's variational inference. And inference is a problem of moving numbers, not multiplying them.

2dc04f232993.en: This part is about running models fast: guessing ahead and checking at once, storing numbers in fewer bits, <bookmark mark='a'/> and moving fewer bytes.
2dc04f232993.zh: 这一部分讲的是怎样让模型跑得快：先猜几步、一次核对，用更少的比特来存数字，<bookmark mark='a'/>以及少搬运一些字节。

30e297332721.en: Chapter one. Guess ahead, check at once.
30e297332721.zh: 第1章。先猜几步，一次核对。

8ce782910fb4.en: A big model writes one token per run, and each run has to read all its billions of weights from memory. That reading, not the arithmetic, is the bottleneck. <bookmark mark='a'/> So let a small, fast model draft a few tokens ahead. <bookmark mark='b'/> Then the big model checks all of them in a single run, since it can score every position at once, the way it does in training. <bookmark mark='c'/> Keep the drafts it agrees with; at the first disagreement, take the big model's choice and start again.
8ce782910fb4.zh: 大模型每运行一次，只能写出一个词元，而且每次都得从内存里读出它那几十亿个权重。瓶颈在于读取，而不在于运算。<bookmark mark='a'/>那就让一个又小又快的模型，先往前起草几个词元。<bookmark mark='b'/>然后，大模型只运行一次，就把它们全部核对一遍：它能同时给每个位置打分，就像训练时那样。<bookmark mark='c'/>它认可的草稿，就留下；碰到第一处分歧，就采用大模型自己的选择，然后从那里重新开始。

24fef77c54d5.en: The clever part is that nothing changes about what the big model says. <bookmark mark='a'/> Here are both guesses for the next character, on our own models: part eleven's transformer as the big one, a small counting model as the draft. <bookmark mark='b'/> Accept a drafted character with probability p over q, capped at one: where the draft guesses a character too often, the excess gets thrown out. <bookmark mark='c'/> If it's rejected, sample from what's left of p after taking q away: exactly the part the draft guessed too rarely. <bookmark mark='d'/> Run the rule two hundred thousand times, and the characters it outputs follow the big model's probabilities exactly, not the draft's: speculative decoding is faster with no change in quality.
24fef77c54d5.zh: 巧妙之处在于，大模型说出的内容，一点都没有变。<bookmark mark='a'/>这是两个模型对下一个字符的猜测，用的是我们自己的模型：第11部分的Transformer当大模型，一个小小的计数模型当草稿模型。<bookmark mark='b'/>草稿里的一个字符，以q分之p的概率被接受，这个概率最大取1：草稿把哪个字符猜得太频繁，多出来的那部分就被扔掉。<bookmark mark='c'/>如果被拒绝，就从p减去q之后剩下的部分里重新采样：恰好是草稿猜得太少的那一部分。<bookmark mark='d'/>把这条规则运行20万次，它输出的字符，完全遵循大模型的概率，而不是草稿的：投机解码更快，质量却丝毫不变。

aeff2d7d9ff8.en: Our little draft is accepted 62 percent of the time. <bookmark mark='a'/> Drafting k characters, the big model writes on average one minus alpha to the k plus one, over one minus alpha, per run: 2.4 with four drafted. Real systems reach two to three times the speed this way, and some models, like DeepSeek-V3, are trained to draft for themselves.
aeff2d7d9ff8.zh: 我们这个小小的草稿模型，有62%的时候被接受。<bookmark mark='a'/>每轮起草k个字符，大模型每运行一次，平均写出的字符数，是1减去α的k加1次方，再除以1减去α：起草4个时，是2.4个。真实的系统靠这个办法，能把速度提高到2到3倍；有些模型，比如DeepSeek-V3，还被训练成自己给自己起草。

44bcc6e5c25b.en: Chapter two. Fewer bits per number.
44bcc6e5c25b.zh: 第2章。每个数少用几个比特。

1ac421f46122.en: The other way to cut memory traffic: store each number in fewer bits. Here are the weights of one layer of our transformer: most near zero, a few larger. <bookmark mark='a'/> With four bits, each weight is rounded to one of fifteen evenly spaced values, the same number either side of zero. <bookmark mark='b'/> The newest chips use FP4 instead: a tiny floating-point number, with more values near zero where the weights crowd, and a shared scale for every block of thirty-two. <bookmark mark='e'/> A float stores a power of two, plus a little detail within it, so its values are packed close near zero and spread further apart away from it. FP4's layout is called E2M1: two bits for the power, one for the detail, and one for the sign.

f6d8c637e895.en: What does it cost? <bookmark mark='a'/> Rounded to eight bits, our transformer is no worse. At four bits, 0.047 bits worse per character, for an eighth of the memory; at three, 0.26 worse: it starts to break. FP4, with its scale for every block of thirty-two, loses only 0.019: better than plain four bits, for the same memory. <bookmark mark='b'/> Big models tolerate rounding even better, the newest are trained in eight or even four bits from the start, and there are better formats, and better ways to round, than the plain ones here.
f6d8c637e895.zh: 代价是多少？<bookmark mark='a'/>取整到8比特，我们的Transformer一点也没变差。到4比特，每个字符差了0.047比特，换来的是只用八分之一的内存；到3比特，差了0.26：它开始崩了。FP4，每32个数配一个缩放因子，只损失0.019：比普通的4比特更好，内存却一样。<bookmark mark='b'/>大模型对取整的容忍度还要更高，最新的模型从一开始就用8比特、甚至4比特训练；而且还有比这里这些朴素做法更好的格式，和更好的取整方法。

4fc0235c4174.en: Two four-bit float formats now matter, and the difference between them is all in the scales. <bookmark mark='a'/> MXFP4, the open standard, shares one scale among thirty-two numbers, and the scale is a pure power of two: cheap to apply, but coarse, so a block's largest weight can land anywhere from four to eight on the E2M1 grid, and past six it's clipped. OpenAI's gpt-oss stores its experts this way. <bookmark mark='b'/> NVFP4, on NVIDIA's Blackwell chips, uses blocks of sixteen, and each scale is itself a small eight-bit float, so it can fit the block's largest weight to six almost exactly; one more scale for the whole weight matrix keeps everything in range. It costs 4.5 bits per weight instead of 4.25. <bookmark mark='c'/> On our transformer: MXFP4 loses 0.026 bits a character, NVFP4 0.024, and plain four-bit integers with a scale per row 0.047. The best here is NVFP4. For comparison, FP4 with an exact scale for every block of thirty-two, from before, lost 0.019: rounding the scale to a power of two is what costs MXFP4 its extra.

9ef90af9a910.en: Two tricks make low precision work much better than plain rounding. The first is GPTQ. <bookmark mark='a'/> Round a layer's weights one input column at a time. <bookmark mark='b'/> Each rounding leaves an error; <bookmark mark='c'/> instead of accepting it, nudge the weights on the inputs not yet rounded, so the layer's output barely changes. How much to nudge comes from H, the inputs' second moment, measured on real text: it records which inputs tend to be big together. If two inputs move together, a rounding error on one can be cancelled by adjusting the other. <bookmark mark='d'/> On a real layer of our transformer, at three bits, the error in its output drops from 17 to 10 percent. <bookmark mark='e'/> The second trick is a rotation. In large models a few weights and activations, the numbers flowing through the network for this particular input, which change with every token while the weights stay fixed, are huge outliers, far bigger than the rest, and one outlier forces a coarse scale on its whole row. <bookmark mark='h'/> Multiply by a Hadamard matrix first, a grid of plus and minus ones. It's orthogonal: a pure rotation, which changes no lengths and can be undone exactly. The outlier is spread evenly over the row, and the rotation is undone afterwards. Our small model has no such outliers: a row's largest weight is only about 2.8 times the typical one, before and after. <bookmark mark='f'/> On our whole transformer at three bits: plain rounding loses 0.255 bits a character, GPTQ only 0.123, and rotating first 0.327, worse: with nothing to spread, it only spreads each rounding error over every input, including the few that carry large activations. Real systems rotate the activations too, so they can be rounded as well, and pair the rotation with GPTQ.

b3f5ede7783c.en: Chapter three. Moving numbers is the cost.
b3f5ede7783c.zh: 第3章。代价在于搬运数字。

03a1224b5402.en: Every computer has two speeds: how fast it does arithmetic, and how fast it moves numbers from memory. <bookmark mark='a'/> We measured this one. The roofline: a slope where moving data is the limit, and a flat roof where arithmetic is. <bookmark mark='b'/> Big matrix products do lots of arithmetic per number moved, and the fastest of them sets the roof. <bookmark mark='c'/> But writing one token at a time multiplies each weight once: about one operation per byte, down on the slope, well below the roof. That's why the tricks of this part all move fewer bytes.
03a1224b5402.zh: 每台计算机都有两种速度：做运算有多快，从内存里搬运数字有多快。<bookmark mark='a'/>我们测了这一台。这就是屋顶线：受限于搬运数据的地方，是一道斜坡；受限于运算的地方，是一片平平的屋顶。<bookmark mark='b'/>大的矩阵乘法，每搬运一个数，都要做很多运算，其中最快的那一个，就定下了屋顶的高度。<bookmark mark='c'/>可是一次写一个词元，每个权重只乘一次：大约每个字节一次运算，落在斜坡上，远在屋顶之下。正因为这样，这一部分的所有技巧，都是为了少搬运一些字节。

7dfe3ee9843e.en: Attention has its own memory problem: the table of scores grows with the square of the length. FlashAttention never stores it. <bookmark mark='a'/> It takes a block of queries, streams the keys and values through in tiles, small enough to stay in the chip's fastest memory, <bookmark mark='b'/> and keeps a running maximum and a running sum: it remembers the biggest score so far, so the exponentials never blow up, and rescales its partial sum whenever a bigger one arrives. So the softmax comes out exactly right at the end. We checked it: the same numbers as the plain formula, to rounding error, without ever holding the table.

1eedb7524aed.en: Finally, the cache from part twelve, on a server answering many people at once. <bookmark mark='a'/> Reserve each conversation one block of memory long enough for the longest possible answer, and most of it sits empty: 79 percent wasted, for our two hundred random requests. <bookmark mark='b'/> vLLM borrowed the operating system's trick: hand out memory in small pages, as each conversation grows. Waste falls to 0.8 percent, so the same chip serves several times as many people.
1eedb7524aed.zh: 最后，是第12部分的那个缓存，放在一台同时回答很多人的服务器上。<bookmark mark='a'/>如果给每段对话预留一整块内存，长到能装下最长的回答，那么大部分都会空着：在我们这200个随机请求上，浪费了79%。<bookmark mark='b'/>vLLM借用了操作系统的老办法：随着每段对话变长，把内存一小页一小页地分给它。浪费降到了0.8%，于是同一块芯片，能服务的人多了好几倍。

62f2e3b06137.en: Let's take stock. Writing one token reads every weight, so memory sets the speed limit. A small model can guess ahead and the big one check its guesses at once, with exactly the same output. Numbers can be stored in eight bits, or four, for little loss. And the roofline says why all of this works: moving bytes is the cost, so FlashAttention computes in tiles and servers hand out memory in pages.
62f2e3b06137.zh: 我们来盘点一下。写一个词元，就要读一遍所有的权重，所以内存决定了速度的上限。小模型可以先往前猜，大模型再一次性核对它的猜测，输出完全不变。数字可以用8个比特、甚至4个比特来存，损失很小。而屋顶线说明了这一切为什么管用：搬运字节才是代价，所以FlashAttention分块计算，服务器按页分配内存。

f1bf7805c741.en: This part paid off ideas from earlier ones. The key-value cache of part twelve is what the pages hold. Mixture-of-experts, from part thirteen, is the same idea as quantization: read fewer bytes per token. And the long chains of thought of parts seventeen and eighteen are why speed matters so much.
f1bf7805c741.zh: 这一部分，兑现了前面几部分的想法。页里装的，正是第12部分的键值缓存。第13部分的混合专家，和量化是同一个想法：每个词元少读一些字节。而第17和第18部分那些长长的思维链，正是速度如此重要的原因。

e65239f0d5e5.en: Next time, the last part: looking inside the model. How a network packs more ideas than it has dimensions, <bookmark mark='a'/> five directions squeezed into a plane, and how to pull them back apart.
e65239f0d5e5.zh: 下一次，是最后一部分：看看模型内部。一个网络，怎样装下比它的维数还多的想法，<bookmark mark='a'/>把5个方向挤进一个平面；又怎样把它们重新拆开。

e57177f092a2.en: Thanks for watching, and see you in the final part.
e57177f092a2.zh: 感谢观看，最后一部分见。
